blocks.text: Within a few milliseconds of a motor neuron firing, a muscle fibre in your forearm has received a chemical message, converted it to an electrical impulse, released a pulse of calcium and begun to shorten. When any one step of that chain is faulty, the result can be weakness, paralysis or rigidity, depending on which step fails. This unit follows the signal from nerve terminal to cross-bridge.

blocks.markdown:
**The neuromuscular junction (NMJ).** Each skeletal muscle fibre is innervated by one motor neuron terminal at the **motor end plate**, a specialised region of sarcolemma with deep folds and a high density of receptors. Transmission here is chemical and uses **acetylcholine (ACh)**.

1. An action potential arrives at the nerve terminal and opens **voltage-gated Ca2+ channels**.
2. Ca2+ enters the terminal and triggers **exocytosis** of ACh-containing synaptic vesicles (via SNARE proteins).
3. ACh diffuses across the **synaptic cleft** and binds **nicotinic acetylcholine receptors**, which are ligand-gated cation channels on the end plate.
4. The channels open, and Na+ enters (and K+ leaves), depolarising the end plate: this local graded depolarisation is the **end-plate potential (EPP)**.
5. The EPP spreads to the adjacent muscle membrane and, if it reaches threshold, opens **voltage-gated Na+ channels** and triggers a **muscle action potential** that propagates along the fibre.
6. **Acetylcholinesterase** in the cleft rapidly breaks ACh down to acetate and choline, ending the signal and allowing choline to be taken back into the terminal.

blocks.title: End-plate potential and safety factor
blocks.text: The end-plate potential is the depolarisation of the motor end plate caused by ACh opening nicotinic receptors. The safety factor is the ratio of the EPP amplitude to the depolarisation needed to reach threshold. In healthy muscle it is greater than 1 (commonly about 2-3), so every nerve impulse reliably triggers a muscle action potential, with a reserve.

blocks.caption: EPP amplitude and the depolarisation required to reach threshold are both in millivolts; transmission fails when the ratio falls below 1.

blocks.title: Safety factor at the end plate
blocks.prompt: A muscle fibre has a resting potential of -90 mV and a threshold of -60 mV. A normal EPP is 60 mV in amplitude. Calculate the safety factor, and then the EPP and safety factor if only 40% of the nicotinic receptors are functional (assume EPP is proportional to the number of functional receptors).

steps.text: With 40% of receptors, the EPP is 0.4 x 60 = 24 mV, so the safety factor is 24/30 = 0.8, which is below 1.
A safety factor below 1 means the EPP does not reach threshold, so the muscle action potential fails and the fibre does not contract.

blocks.answer: Normal safety factor is 2.0; with 40% of receptors it falls to 0.8 and transmission fails.

blocks.markdown:
**Excitation-contraction coupling (ECC).** ECC is the process linking the muscle action potential to contraction.

1. The action potential spreads along the sarcolemma and down the **transverse (T) tubules**, invaginations that carry it deep into the fibre.
2. In the T-tubule membrane, the voltage-sensing **dihydropyridine receptor (DHPR, an L-type Ca2+ channel)** changes conformation.
3. In skeletal muscle, DHPR is **mechanically linked** to the **ryanodine receptor (RyR1)**, a Ca2+ release channel on the terminal cisterna of the **sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR)**; the conformational change opens RyR1. (Skeletal muscle does not need extracellular Ca2+ entry for this step.)
4. **Ca2+ floods into the cytosol** from the SR.
5. Ca2+ binds **troponin C** on the thin filament; this moves **tropomyosin** away from the **myosin-binding sites** on actin.
6. Myosin heads bind actin and cycle.

**The cross-bridge cycle.** (1) A myosin head with bound ADP and phosphate is attached to actin. (2) Release of phosphate and ADP drives the **power stroke**, in which the head swivels and pulls the thin filament towards the centre of the sarcomere. (3) Binding of a new **ATP** to myosin causes it to **detach** from actin. (4) Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate re-**cocks** the head, which can bind again if Ca2+ is still bound to troponin. Without ATP, heads stay attached (rigor, as in rigor mortis). **Relaxation** occurs when Ca2+ is pumped back into the SR by the **SERCA** Ca2+-ATPase; Ca2+ dissociates from troponin, and tropomyosin blocks the actin sites again. Calsequestrin inside the SR stores calcium.

blocks.caption: Sequence of events from nerve to contraction and examples of disruption.
rows: Myasthenia gravis; curare (competitive antagonist, pharmacology example)

blocks.markdown: **Myasthenia gravis.** In myasthenia gravis, autoantibodies (IgG) are directed against the **nicotinic acetylcholine receptor** at the end plate (less often against related proteins such as MuSK). They cause **fewer functional receptors** through receptor cross-linking and internalisation, complement-mediated damage to the end-plate folds and receptor blockade. Each ACh release now produces a **smaller EPP** and a reduced safety factor. At rest the EPP may still reach threshold, but with repeated activity ACh release per impulse declines (normal 'run-down' of the readily releasable pool), so the EPP falls below threshold in some fibres and transmission fails. The result is **fatigable weakness**: ptosis (drooping eyelids), diplopia, difficulty chewing and swallowing, and limb weakness that worsens with use and in the evening and improves with rest. **Anticholinesterase** drugs (pharmacology teaching example) block acetylcholinesterase, so ACh remains longer in the cleft and the EPP is larger. Thymic abnormalities are commonly associated.

blocks.title: Explaining fatigability
blocks.prompt: A patient with myasthenia gravis has an EPP amplitude of 36 mV when rested and a threshold depolarisation of 30 mV. After repeated nerve stimulation, ACh release falls to 70% of the initial value. Does transmission still succeed?

steps.text: After rundown, EPP is 0.70 x 36 = 25.2 mV, giving a safety factor of 25.2/30 = 0.84.
A safety factor below 1 means the EPP no longer reaches threshold, so the fibre fails to fire.
A healthy person with a safety factor of about 2-3 has enough reserve to tolerate the same 30% fall and still fire.

blocks.answer: Transmission initially succeeds (safety factor 1.2) but fails after repeated use (0.84), explaining fatigable weakness.

items: Motor neuron action potential opens presynaptic Ca2+ channels; ACh is released.
ACh binds nicotinic receptors, producing the end-plate potential, which triggers a muscle action potential.
T-tubule DHPR activates RyR1, releasing Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Ca2+ binds troponin C, exposing actin sites and allowing cross-bridge cycling with ATP.
SERCA pumps Ca2+ back into the SR and the muscle relaxes.

blocks.title: Calcium plays two different roles
blocks.text: At the nerve terminal, Ca2+ entering through voltage-gated channels triggers ACh release. In the muscle fibre, Ca2+ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds troponin C and triggers contraction. Skeletal muscle ECC does not depend on calcium entering from outside the fibre.

blocks.title: ATP detaches, it does not power the attachment
blocks.text: A common error is to say ATP is needed for myosin to bind actin. ATP binding releases myosin from actin; its hydrolysis re-cocks the head. The power stroke follows binding of the cocked head to actin and release of phosphate.

points: ACh released from the motor nerve terminal after Ca2+ entry binds nicotinic receptors to produce an end-plate potential that normally exceeds threshold (a safety factor above 1).

Acetylcholinesterase terminates transmission; the muscle action potential travels down the T-tubules and the DHPR activates the ryanodine receptor RyR1 to release Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Ca2+ binds troponin C, moving tropomyosin and allowing cross-bridge cycling; ATP detaches myosin and SERCA reuptake of Ca2+ produces relaxation.
In myasthenia gravis, antibodies reduce functional nicotinic receptors, lowering the EPP and safety factor so transmission fails with repeated use (fatigable weakness).

questions.stem: Which receptor mediates the end-plate potential at the skeletal neuromuscular junction?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: it is a ligand-gated cation channel on the motor end plate.
distractorRationale.b: Muscarinic receptors are G-protein-coupled receptors in smooth muscle, glands and heart.
distractorRationale.c: Adrenergic receptors are not involved in end-plate transmission.
distractorRationale.d: The ryanodine receptor is the sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ release channel.

questions.explanation: ACh binds nicotinic receptors, which are ligand-gated channels permeable to Na+ and K+. The net inward Na+ current depolarises the end plate to produce the end-plate potential.

questions.stem: Which event directly triggers the release of acetylcholine from the motor nerve terminal?

options.text: Ca2+ entry through voltage-gated Ca2+ channels
Binding of ACh to presynaptic muscarinic receptors

questions.correctOptionText: Ca2+ entry through voltage-gated Ca2+ channels

distractorRationale.b: Nicotinic receptors are on the postsynaptic membrane.
distractorRationale.c: This is not the primary trigger for release.
distractorRationale.d: Acetylcholinesterase terminates, not triggers, the signal.

questions.explanation: The action potential opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in the nerve terminal. The rise in intracellular Ca2+ triggers SNARE-mediated fusion of ACh vesicles with the membrane. Botulinum toxin blocks this step.

questions.stem: In skeletal muscle excitation-contraction coupling, how does the T-tubule action potential cause release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum?

options.text: Voltage-sensing dihydropyridine receptors mechanically open the ryanodine receptors
Ca2+ entering through the sarcolemma binds the ryanodine receptor
ACh diffuses into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Troponin C releases Ca2+ into the T-tubule

questions.correctOptionText: Voltage-sensing dihydropyridine receptors mechanically open the ryanodine receptors

distractorRationale.a: Correct: in skeletal muscle the coupling is direct and mechanical.
distractorRationale.b: Skeletal muscle ECC does not require extracellular Ca2+ entry (unlike cardiac muscle).
distractorRationale.c: ACh does not enter the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
distractorRationale.d: Troponin C binds Ca2+; it does not release it into T-tubules.

questions.explanation: The dihydropyridine receptor in the T-tubule senses depolarisation and changes conformation. It is physically coupled to RyR1 on the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which opens and releases Ca2+ into the cytosol.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has drooping eyelids and double vision that worsen towards the evening and after prolonged reading, and improve after rest. Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies are detected. What best explains the fatigable weakness?

options.text: Fewer functional receptors give a small end-plate potential that falls below threshold as ACh release declines with repeated use
Excess acetylcholinesterase activity breaks down ACh before it reaches the muscle
Failure of the sarcoplasmic reticulum to store calcium
Failure of the motor nerve to conduct action potentials

questions.correctOptionText: Fewer functional receptors give a small end-plate potential that falls below threshold as ACh release declines with repeated use

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the reduced safety factor lets transmission fail with use.
distractorRationale.b: Acetylcholinesterase is not excessive in this condition.
distractorRationale.c: The calcium store is not the defect.
distractorRationale.d: The nerve conducts normally; the defect is at the end plate.

questions.explanation: Autoantibodies reduce the number of functional nicotinic receptors, so the EPP is smaller and the safety factor lower. With repeated activity ACh release falls, so EPPs fail to reach threshold in more fibres, causing weakness that improves with rest.

questions.stem: Binding of a new ATP molecule to the myosin head causes myosin to detach from actin.
questions.explanation: ATP binding releases myosin from actin; hydrolysis then re-cocks the head. When ATP is depleted, as after death, heads remain attached and the muscle is stiff (rigor).

questions.stem: A muscle fibre has a resting potential of -90 mV and a threshold of -58 mV. A normal end-plate potential has an amplitude of 64 mV. Calculate the safety factor (EPP amplitude divided by the depolarisation needed to reach threshold).
questions.explanation: The depolarisation needed is -58 - (-90) = 32 mV. The safety factor is 64/32 = 2.0, meaning the EPP is twice the minimum required, giving a reserve so that each nerve impulse reliably triggers a muscle action potential.

questions.stem: In a patient with myasthenia gravis, only 35% of the nicotinic receptors are functional. Assuming EPP amplitude is proportional to the number of functional receptors, and the normal EPP is 64 mV, what is the EPP amplitude in mV? (The depolarisation needed to reach threshold is 32 mV.)
questions.explanation: The EPP is 0.35 x 64 = 22.4 mV. This is below the 32 mV needed to reach threshold (safety factor 0.7), so transmission fails, which explains weakness in this condition.

questions.stem: Describe the sequence of events at the neuromuscular junction from arrival of the nerve action potential to generation of a muscle action potential, including termination of the signal.
markingGuide: Nerve terminal depolarisation opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels
Ca2+ entry triggers exocytosis of ACh vesicles into the synaptic cleft
ACh binds nicotinic receptors on the motor end plate (ligand-gated cation channels)
Na+ entry produces the end-plate potential, a graded local depolarisation
EPP exceeds threshold (safety factor above 1) and opens voltage-gated Na+ channels, generating a muscle action potential
Acetylcholinesterase degrades ACh to acetate and choline, ending the signal; choline is recycled
questions.explanation: Neuromuscular transmission is a one-to-one chemical relay with a large safety margin. Each step is a potential site for drugs, toxins or disease.

questions.stem: Outline excitation-contraction coupling in skeletal muscle from the muscle action potential to relaxation, explaining the roles of calcium, troponin and ATP in the cross-bridge cycle.
markingGuide: Action potential spreads along the sarcolemma and into T-tubules
Dihydropyridine receptor senses depolarisation and mechanically opens the ryanodine receptor (RyR1) on the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Ca2+ is released into the cytosol
Ca2+ binds troponin C, moving tropomyosin to expose myosin-binding sites on actin
Cross-bridge cycle: myosin binds actin, power stroke with release of phosphate and ADP, ATP binds and detaches the head, hydrolysis re-cocks it
Relaxation: SERCA pumps Ca2+ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, Ca2+ leaves troponin and tropomyosin re-blocks actin
Without ATP, heads remain attached (rigor)
questions.explanation: Calcium is the link between excitation and contraction, and ATP drives both the cycle and the calcium reuptake that ends it. Each of these steps explains a characteristic clinical or experimental finding.

questions.stem: Explain how myasthenia gravis impairs neuromuscular transmission, why the weakness is fatigable and worse at the end of the day, and why an anticholinesterase drug improves it (pharmacology teaching example).
markingGuide: Autoantibodies against nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the end plate
Fewer functional receptors through receptor blockade, internalisation and complement-mediated damage to the end-plate folds
Smaller end-plate potential and reduced safety factor
With repeated activity ACh release per impulse falls (rundown), so the EPP falls below threshold in more fibres and transmission fails
Weakness is therefore fatigable (ptosis, diplopia, bulbar weakness) and improves with rest
Anticholinesterase inhibitors slow breakdown of ACh in the cleft, increasing ACh concentration and the EPP
Thymic abnormalities are associated
questions.explanation: The disease lowers the margin of safety at each synapse until it is critical. Fatigue appears when normal fall in transmitter release pushes the already small EPP below threshold.
